Monitoring
a model service

Prometheus and Grafana — for the six months after you ship.

Who this is for

  • You have a service in production (sessions 3 and 4) and no idea how it is behaving.
  • Your current monitoring is someone saying "it seems slow today".
  • You have never written PromQL and are not sure what a histogram is for.

By the end you can

  • Instrument a service with counters, histograms and gauges — and know which to use
  • Run Prometheus and Grafana, and provision a dashboard from files
  • Write the four queries you will actually use
  • Alert on a model drifting, not only on the server dying

Companion notebook: monitoring_tutorial.ipynb.

The problem — nothing crashes

The old way was an ssh session, tail -f and a CPU graph per machine. None of those notices the failure a model service actually has.

Three questions, and who can answer them

Is it up?

Any health check. Solved for decades.

Is it fast, and failing?

Needs metrics with history — this is the Prometheus part.

Is it still right?

Needs the prediction distribution, and eventually labels. Nothing gives you this by default.

A model service needs all three. Most teams have the first, buy the second, and never build the third — which is the one that decays.

Crash course — how Prometheus sees the world

WordWhat it means
metricone named number your service publishes, e.g. api_requests_total.
labela tag attached to a metric — status="500". One metric with labels replaces a dozen separate metrics.
scrapePrometheus pulling your /metrics page on a timer. Your app never sends anything anywhere.
PromQLthe query language you ask questions in, e.g. rate(api_requests_total[1m]).
alert rulea PromQL expression plus "and it has to stay true for this long" — the part that stops one bad second from paging someone.

How Prometheus is put together

Diagram: Prometheus documentation (prometheus.io) — Apache 2.0

Follow pull metrics on the left: the server reaches out on a timer and stores what it finds. Everything else reads from there — Grafana asks in PromQL, and Alertmanager turns a rule that went true into an email or a page.

The three metric types

Instrumenting, in one middleware

Three metrics and one wrapper. Every request is counted and timed without touching a single endpoint.

from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram, Gauge, generate_latest

REQUESTS = Counter("api_requests_total", "requests", ["endpoint", "method", "status"])
LATENCY  = Histogram("api_request_duration_seconds", "duration", ["endpoint"],
                    buckets=(.001, .005, .01, .025, .05, .1, .25, .5, 1, 2.5))
INFLIGHT = Gauge("api_inflight_requests", "being handled right now")

@app.middleware("http")
async def observe(request, call_next):
    INFLIGHT.inc()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        response = await call_next(request); return response
    finally:
        INFLIGHT.dec()
        LATENCY.labels(endpoint=request.url.path).observe(time.perf_counter() - t0)
        REQUESTS.labels(endpoint=request.url.path, method=request.method,
                        status=str(response.status_code)).inc()

@app.get("/metrics")
def metrics(): return Response(generate_latest(), media_type=CONTENT_TYPE_LATEST)
PartWhat it does
Counteronly ever goes up; you ask for its rate later, never its value
Histogram bucketsthe boundaries you choose; percentiles can only be as precise as these
Gaugegoes up and down — a number that is true right now, like requests in flight
["endpoint", "method", "status"]labels: one series per combination. Never put a user id here, or the series explode
@app.middleware("http")wraps every request, so no endpoint has to remember to measure itself

Set your own buckets. The defaults reach 10 seconds, which is useless for an API answering in 15 ms — every request lands in the first bucket and your p95 is meaningless.

Labels: useful, until they multiply

A label with a few values is free. A label containing a user id creates a new time series per user, and that is how monitoring bills explode.

# good: a handful of values
REQUESTS.labels(endpoint="/predict", method="POST", status="200")

# disaster: unbounded
REQUESTS.labels(user_id="48219")          # one time series per user
REQUESTS.labels(request_id=uuid4().hex)   # one per request, forever

Every distinct combination of label values is a separate time series stored forever. This is called cardinality, and it is how people take Prometheus down.

Label onNever label on
endpoint, method, status, model versionuser id, request id, email, raw path with ids

A rough rule: if you cannot name every possible value, it is not a label.

Prometheus pulls; you do not push

You list the addresses to scrape and how often. Your application never sends anything — it just leaves a page for Prometheus to read.

# prometheus.yml
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s

rule_files: [/etc/prometheus/alerts.yml]

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: churn-api
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["api:8000"]      # the service name, not localhost
PartWhat it does
scrape_interval: 15show often it reads every target; your rate([1m]) has to be wider than this
rule_fileswhere the alert rules live, evaluated on the same clock
job_namea label on every series it collects here, so you can ask "which job?"
targets: ["api:8000"]the service name on the docker network, not localhost — localhost is Prometheus itself
  • Prometheus fetches /metrics on a schedule and stores the series.
  • Your app keeps counters in memory; it never talks to Prometheus.
  • If the app restarts, counters reset — and rate() understands that.
  • Cannot edit the thing you want to watch — a database, a queue, the host itself? Run an exporter beside it: a small process that reads it and publishes /metrics on its behalf. Your own service never needs one; you instrumented it directly.

The first query to run, always: up. If it is 0, nothing else on your dashboard means anything.

The four queries you will actually use

Four PromQL expressions covering almost every dashboard: how much traffic, how many errors, how slow typically, and how slow for the unlucky.

# 1. throughput
sum(rate(api_requests_total[1m]))                          5.26 req/s

# 2. error ratio -- a share, not a count
sum(rate(api_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[1m]))
  / sum(rate(api_requests_total[1m]))                      1.1%

# 3. a percentile, from the histogram buckets
histogram_quantile(0.95,
  sum(rate(api_request_duration_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (le))   43.8 ms

# 4. the ML one: mean of a histogram
sum(rate(model_score_sum[5m])) / sum(rate(model_score_count[5m]))   0.647
PartWhat it does
rate(...[1m])per-second increase over the last minute, and it handles a restart to zero
sum(...)add the per-series rates together, or you get one line per label combination
{status=~"5.."}a regex label match: every 5xx status
histogram_quantile(0.95, ... by (le))percentile from bucket counts; by (le) keeps the bucket boundary, which it needs
_sum / _counta histogram ships both, so their ratio is the mean — the ML question

Every number there was measured in the notebook against a live Prometheus scraping a live service.

rate before sum, never the other way round — summing counters across restarts then taking a rate gives you nonsense.

What Grafana actually is

It stores nothing. Grafana asks a data source a query and draws the answer.

Open source or Cloud, same files. The Grafana in this session is the open-source server, running in a container next to Prometheus. Grafana Cloud is the same product hosted for you — the dashboard JSON you are about to write does not change.

Metrics, logs and traces

Three kinds of evidence, in the order worth adopting them.

PillarOne row of it isAnswersCost
metrica number at a point in time, with labels is it happening, and how much?tiny — cheap to keep for a year
loga line of text about one event what exactly happened in that request?large — the bill grows with traffic
traceone request's path across services, timed which hop spent the time?sampled, because keeping all of it is not affordable
This session is metrics only — a counter and a histogram answer what you get paged about. Logs and traces are the same shape, and Grafana reads them too; nothing extra is installed here.
The order people get wrong: traces before a single alert on the error ratio. Metrics are the half that tells you that something is wrong.

The dashboard, provisioned from files

Nobody clicked that together. A datasource YAML and a dashboard JSON, both in the repo, mounted into the container. It can be reviewed in a pull request and recreated from scratch — unlike a dashboard someone built by hand and then left.

The fourth panel is the one an ML team needs

mean predicted probability, phase 1 (normal traffic) : 0.496
mean predicted probability, phase 2 (drifted traffic): 0.860

Same code. Same 200 OK on every request. Same latency. The inputs changed, and the only thing that noticed was the prediction distribution.

Drift, measured

This is the panel a web-ops dashboard does not have, and the one that would have told you three weeks earlier.

PART 02Alerting

Being told, instead of looking.

A rule that fires

A condition plus a duration. for: 30s is what stops one bad second from waking someone up.

groups:
  - name: churn-api
    rules:
      - alert: HighErrorRate
        expr: |
          sum(rate(api_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[1m]))
            / sum(rate(api_requests_total[1m])) > 0.05
        for: 10s                      # sustained, not a single scrape
        labels: {severity: critical}
        annotations:
          summary: "over 5% of requests are failing"
PartWhat it does
alert: HighErrorRatethe name that appears in the alert, and in the page at 3am
exprany PromQL that returns a value; a result that is non-empty and true is a firing instance
for: 10sit must stay true this long — pending until then, which is what kills flapping
labels: {severity}how Alertmanager decides where to send it
annotations: {summary}the human sentence; the labels route, the annotations explain
alerts now: [('HighErrorRate', 'firing')]

Measured, not described: the notebook sends 60 failing requests and waits for the rule to move from inactive to pending to firing.

for: is not optional. A condition true for one scrape is noise. Without it you will silence the alert within a week, and then it protects nothing.

What to alert on — and what not to

AlertDo not alert
error ratio above threshold, sustaineda single failed request
p95 latency against your real SLOa p99 spike at 3am with no users
up == 0 — it is unreachableCPU at 80% — that is a graph
predictions far from the training distributionevery small wobble
deployed model version ≠ expecteddisk at 60%

The test for every alert: what would I do at 3am? If the answer is "look at it in the morning", it is a dashboard panel, not a page.

What monitoring a model adds

QuestionMetricWhy it is invisible otherwise
Have the inputs moved?feature summaries, or the score meanthe service answers perfectly
Have the predictions moved?model_score histogramstill 200, every time
Is it still accurate?needs labels, which arrive lateryou cannot measure it live

That third row is the honest limit. Ground truth arrives days or weeks after the prediction, so you monitor proxies now and reconcile with labels later.

Do not let "we cannot measure accuracy live" become "we measure nothing". The score distribution is free, and it moves first.

Cheat sheet

# instrument
Counter("x_total", "help", ["label"]).labels(...).inc()
Histogram("x_seconds", "help", buckets=(...)).observe(dt)
Gauge("x_now", "help").set(v) / .inc() / .dec()
@app.get("/metrics") -> Response(generate_latest(), media_type=CONTENT_TYPE_LATEST)

# scrape (prometheus.yml)
scrape_configs: [{job_name: api, static_configs: [{targets: ["api:8000"]}]}]

# query
up                                                  # check this first
sum(rate(x_total[1m])) by (endpoint)                # rate BEFORE sum
sum(rate(x_total{status=~"5.."}[1m])) / sum(rate(x_total[1m]))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(x_bucket[1m])) by (le))
sum(rate(score_sum[5m])) / sum(rate(score_count[5m]))   # mean of a histogram

# alert
- alert: Name
  expr: ...
  for: 5m                                           # never omit this

Start tomorrow, in this order

  1. Add /metrics to one service. One middleware, three metrics, half an hour.
  2. Set the histogram buckets to your real latencies. The defaults are wrong for an API.
  3. Four panels: throughput, error ratio, p95, and one model-specific number.
  4. Write one alert — error ratio, with a for: — and check it reaches a human.
  5. Commit the dashboard JSON. A dashboard you cannot recreate is a dashboard you will lose.
  6. Only then add drift detection.
